content.text: In everyday language, "work" might mean doing homework or going to a job. In physics, work has a very specific meaning: it's the energy transferred when a force moves an object. Understanding work helps us connect forces to energy changes.
Work done (W = Fd) is the energy transferred when a force causes an object to move. The distance must be measured in the direction of the force. 1 joule = 1 newton x 1 metre.
is done when a force causes an object to move in the direction of the force.
A force must act on the object
There must be a component of force in the direction of movement
The object doesn't move (even if force is applied)
The force is perpendicular to the movement
No force acts on the object
Carrying a box horizontally (gravity is vertical, movement is horizontal)
An object floating in space at constant velocity
= distance moved in direction of force (m)
One joule is the work done when a force of 1 newton moves an object 1 metre.
When force is at angle θ to the direction of movement:
= angle between force and direction of motion
: W = Fd (force in direction of motion)
Positive work: energy transferred TO the object
Negative work: energy transferred FROM the object
A force of 50 N pushes a box 4 m across a floor. Calculate the work done.
A crane lifts a 200 kg crate through a height of 15 m. How much work is done against gravity? (g = 10 N/kg)
A person carries a 100 N box horizontally for 20 m. How much work is done against gravity?
The force (weight) acts vertically, but movement is horizontal. Force is perpendicular to motion, so no work is done against gravity.
(Note: Work IS done by the person's muscles, but not against gravity.)
A force of 80 N is applied at 60° to the horizontal. The object moves 5 m horizontally. Calculate the work done.
A braking force of 3000 N stops a car over 20 m. How much kinetic energy did the car lose?
This is negative work (force opposes motion), so the car loses 60 kJ of kinetic energy.
This equals the gain in gravitational potential energy.
This energy is transferred to thermal energy (heat).
This equals the elastic potential energy stored.
The area under a force-distance graph equals the work done.
Shaded area = Work done = F x d
For a constant force: Area = rectangle = F × d
For a varying force: Calculate the area under the curve (may involve triangles, trapeziums, or integration).
The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy:
This connects force, distance, and velocity.
When the force and movement are not in the same direction, use W = Fd cos(theta). If the force is perpendicular to movement (theta = 90 degrees), cos(90) = 0, so no work is done.
Climbing stairs does work against gravity
Escalators and lifts do work for us
Input work = useful output work + wasted work
Machines can multiply force but not work
No machine can output more work than is put in
Engines do work to accelerate vehicles
Brakes do negative work to decelerate vehicles
Friction constantly requires work to overcome

Work done against friction is transferred to thermal energy stores. Work done against gravity is transferred to gravitational potential energy stores. In both cases, work done equals energy transferred.
— In physics, no work is done if there's no movement, even if it feels tiring. Your muscles do internal work, but not on the object.
— Work depends on both force AND distance. A small force over a large distance can do more work than a large force over a small distance.
— Work can be negative when force opposes motion (like friction slowing an object).
"If I walk in a circle and return to the start, no work was done"
— Work was done against friction. Net work might be zero against gravity, but not overall.
— Joules are the unit for both energy and work. Work IS energy transfer.
